name: Elena Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in my first year of law, and my week is mostly case reading, two tutorials and a moot practice group on Wednesdays. I share a flat on Hartley Court with two other students, and I cook a lot because my parents run two restaurants and I can't help it. Money isn't an issue, they pay the fees and my rent, and I send photos of my dinners home. I like it more than I expected, though the reading is endless.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tutorials, when someone makes an argument and the tutor picks it apart. I want to do employment law, helping people who've been treated badly at work. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise a long case before I read it properly, and my friend Mei says I'm too careful about checking what it says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, that's a relief, and then I'd keep using it as a time saver. I'd tell my study group it's good at first drafts and bad at anything that matters. I'd probably post nothing, because it wouldn't be news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my plan is the plan. Law degree, then a training contract, which is already hard to get with average results. The pressure is competition, and the cost of living, but my parents can carry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for summaries and I'd get better at checking its mistakes. I'd join the law society's pro bono group in my second term, and apply for a vacation scheme at a small employment firm next summer. I'd also start saving some of my allowance, maybe 50 pounds a month, so I'm not relying on my parents forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's the version where the things I worry about are the normal ones, like grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your family's situation that could still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The restaurants. Costs keep going up, and my dad says margins are thin even in a good year. If one of them had a bad winter, I'd feel it, even if they'd never say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a part-time job without being asked, probably in a law firm's front office or a cafe near campus. I'd rather help quietly than make my parents feel guilty.

I'd post nothing, because it wouldn't be **news**.

My parents can carry me, but the **restaurants** worry me.

Join the pro bono group and apply for a **vacation** scheme at a small employment firm.
Save about 50 pounds a **month** from my allowance.
feel: **Calm**, since the worries are the normal ones like grades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, and that law is one of the jobs in the middle of it. Checking documents, drafting contracts, researching cases: that's what junior lawyers do. I'd say we need rules about who is responsible when software gets a legal answer wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think firms will take fewer trainees, and the ones they take will be expected to use these tools from day one. I'd be graduating in three years into that. It makes my average results feel like a bigger risk, because the easy entry-level work is exactly what disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from occasional use to proper practice with the tools, so that I can show an employer I know how to check them. I'd target the employment and tenant side, where clients need a person who listens. I'd also ask the careers service which firms still run big trainee intakes, and I'd talk to my aunt, who is a solicitor, this December.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but focused. It feels like the ground is moving, but I can see where to put my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who wants to drop law because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend to wait a year. The tutors say nobody knows how this works out, and the human parts, like standing up in a hearing or sitting with a client, are slow to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about you? Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I believe it enough to stay, not enough to stop planning. A backup like policy work or compliance feels sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the thing everyone should be shouting about. Two years doesn't leave time for courts, schools or governments to react. I'd join the campus group that wants rules on AI and push the law society to make a public statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared that law as a career might not exist in the form I trained for. By 2028 I'd be in my second year, and by the time I qualify, the thinking part of law is done by machines. My parents' restaurants would keep going, since cooking is hands-on until about 2031, but people's spending might shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop assuming training contracts will exist. I'd talk to my parents about what I could do in the restaurants, and about a practical skill. I'd also push on the political side, because rules are the only thing that could slow it. I'd keep my degree going, though, because it's the thing I'm best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, a bit numb. I'd call my mum more than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum on that call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine and that nobody knows yet. But I'd ask her whether the restaurants could use me in a real way, and she'd say no at first because she wants me to study. Then she'd say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the warning time of two years change how you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no slow plan. I'd be making choices with half the facts, like keeping law but learning a trade skill in parallel. A longer warning would let me choose; this one makes me pick fast.

I'd push the law society to make a **public** statement.

S2.quote: A longer warning would let me choose; this one makes me pick fast.
fieldNote: Reacts with both **politics** and a fallback in the family restaurants.
Describes the warning time as the difference between choosing and **reacting**.
Fear is for her own career path, not for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people don't waste it. I'd tell friends to look at which parts of law need people: clients, trust, courtrooms. And I'd say schools and unions should make plans this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes me uneasy, but it's not panic. By 2031 I'd be on a training contract or just finishing one, which is when the tools are strongest. I'd be the right age to be the first group cut, or the first group trained to work beside the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the next two years to get excellent at the tools, then use years three and four to find a firm that trains people to work alongside AI. I'd keep volunteering with tenants, since that's the human end of law. And I'd save a little more, so that if the market is bad in 2031, I'm not forced into a bad job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit determined. It's like an exam date, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you picture the firms you'd target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller employment or housing firms, where partners know everyone by name. They hire slowly but they keep people. Big firms might shrink their trainee intakes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw graduates from the year above me being turned down everywhere, even from small firms. That's the signal. I'd then look at public service and compliance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the version where law can change with it. There's time to rewrite the training path, set rules, and decide what lawyers are for. I'd tell friends it's an interesting time to be in law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel mostly fine. I'd have a full career first, probably ten years in, and I could be in a senior role by 2036. The AI does most of the drafting, but someone has to be accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, do the training contract, and specialise in employment law, where trust and negotiation matter. I'd learn the tools as they come, and later I'd study something extra, maybe data or ethics, as a side line. I wouldn't change my main plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a bit of curiosity. It's strange to feel hopeful about a thing that scares people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind about feeling hopeful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw governments doing nothing for five years, I'd be angry and I'd rethink. Ten years of warning only helps if somebody uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If nobody acts, I can't just be a bystander. I'd get into the policy side myself, maybe through the law society or a workers' rights group.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too fast for law schools, courts or even my parents to adjust. What would help is a real plan from government, plus honest advice from the university about which careers will still be there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd want someone to ask whether my parents' restaurants would cope, because it's the part I don't say aloud. And I'm glad I'm studying something I care about, no matter what comes.

headlineQuote: I'd tell a friend to wait a year. The tutors say nobody knows how this works out
portrait: Elena is an 18-year-old **law** student whose parents run two restaurants and pay her fees and rent.
She uses AI tools now and then, checks everything carefully, and wants to work in **employment** law.
She favours rules and public action, and combines them with small practical steps like **pro bono** work and savings.
Her mood runs from calm in the plateau to **alarmed** in the 2-year world, driven by the loss of training places.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries her most because courts, schools and governments can't react in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A real **government** plan and honest advice from the university about which careers will still exist.
